nameStory: This aster is named after Johann Christian Daniel von Schreber, an 18th-century German botanist who described many North American plants. It's also called nettle-leaved Michaelmas-daisy because its leaves have a rough, nettle-like texture and it blooms around Michaelmas (late September), a traditional harvest festival.
description: Schreber's Wood Aster is a perennial wildflower that produces clusters of small white daisy-like flowers with bright yellow centers. This woodland aster typically grows 2-4 feet tall with a somewhat open, branching appearance. It's a rare find in New England forests, preferring shaded areas where it quietly brightens the understory in late summer and early fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White ray petals (usually 8-15) surround bright yellow disc centers, each flower head about 3/4 inch across, clustered in loose, open arrangements at stem tips

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to broadly oval leaves with prominent veins and a rough, sandpaper-like texture that feels scratchy when rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 2-4 feet tall with a somewhat sparse, open branching pattern, often leaning toward available light in shaded areas

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems feel rough to the touch and may have small hairs, becoming more branched toward the top where flower clusters form

habitat: Found in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests, often in partial shade under maples, oaks, and other hardwoods. Prefers well-drained but moisture-retentive woodland soils with good organic matter. In New England, it's extremely rare and may be limited to scattered locations in undisturbed forest areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the forest floor warms, with young leaves appearing fuzzy and heart-shaped. Plants remain low and leafy through the season.
seasonality.summer: Continues vegetative growth with the characteristic rough-textured leaves becoming more prominent. Flower buds begin forming in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak bloom occurs in late summer through early fall, typically August through September, when white flowers create bright spots in the dimming forest understory.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving no visible trace above soil. Roots remain alive underground, ready to resprout in spring.

funFact: This aster is so rare in New England that it's possibly extinct in Maine and has been spotted only 11 times across the entire region, making it one of the most elusive wildflowers you could encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with White Wood Aster, but Schreber's has much rougher, more sandpaper-like leaves and a sparser growth habit. Remember: if the leaves feel really scratchy and rough, you might have found the rare Schreber's rather than the smoother-leaved White Wood Aster.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse wood asters (Eurybia) with the more common fall asters (Symphyotrichum) - wood asters are generally woodland plants with broader leaves, while fall asters prefer open areas and have narrower leaves. The genus name was changed from Aster to Eurybia in recent years based on genetic studies.
compareHints: Among wood asters, Schreber's is distinguished by its extremely rough leaf texture - much rougher than White Wood Aster's smooth leaves or Large-leaved Aster's softer, fuzzy leaves. Its sparse, open growth habit also sets it apart from the denser clusters of Purple Wood Aster. The combination of rough leaves and white flowers in a woodland setting is the key identifying feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its wood aster relatives, white wood aster is the only one with the distinctive serpentine stem pattern.

Among the wood asters, large-leaved aster is easily distinguished by its oversized basal leaves - white wood aster has much smaller, narrow leaves, while Schreber's wood aster has more elongated leaves.
Purple wood aster stands out from its wood aster relatives by having the most vibrant purple flowers - white wood aster is obviously white, while large-leaved aster has much bigger, broader leaves.
Among its wood aster relatives, rough wood aster is the wetland specialist with the distinctive sandpapery leaves.

Among its wood aster relatives, slender aster stands out for its narrow, upright form while white wood aster spreads wider with heart-shaped leaves, and large-leaved aster has distinctively broad foliage.
